diagnosticSteps: Visual inspect capacitor for bulging, leaking, or burn marks
Disconnect power and discharge capacitor safely
Use multimeter on capacitance mode (μF setting)
Compare reading to rating printed on capacitor
Acceptable range: within ±6% of rated value
If dual-run cap: test both HERM (compressor) and FAN sides separately
Common rated values - compressor side: 35-60μF, fan side: 5-10μF
rootCauses: Age/heat degradation (most common - caps last 5-15 years)
Electrical surges or lightning
Overheating from restricted airflow around condenser
Wrong replacement capacitor installed previously
entries.repairProcedure: Replace with exact same μF and voltage rating. Use 370V or 440V rated. Match HERM/FAN/COM terminals. Always discharge old cap before handling. Verify amp draw after replacement.
commonMistakes: Not discharging capacitor before testing - shock hazard
Installing wrong μF rating - causes motor overheating
Not checking amp draw after replacement to verify fix
Assuming compressor is bad without testing cap first

diagnosticSteps: Connect gauges - check suction and discharge pressures
Compare to saturation temp for refrigerant type at current ambient
Calculate superheat: suction line temp minus suction saturation temp
High superheat (>15°F on TXV, >25°F on piston) confirms low charge
Calculate subcooling: condensing temp minus liquid line temp
Low subcooling (<5°F on TXV) also indicates low charge
Check for obvious leak signs: oil stains at joints, service valves, evap coil
Use electronic leak detector at all brazed joints, flare connections, Schrader valves
Check evaporator and condenser coils for micro-leaks
UV dye test for hard-to-find leaks
rootCauses: Leak at brazed joint (most common - vibration fatigue)
Leaking Schrader valve core
Evaporator coil leak (corrosion from formicary corrosion or galvanic corrosion)
Condenser coil leak (lawn mower damage, corrosion)
Flare connection leak (improper torque or damaged flare)
Factory charge insufficient for long line sets
Previous tech did not weigh in charge properly
entries.repairProcedure: 1. Find and repair leak first - NEVER just add refrigerant without leak repair. 2. Recover remaining charge. 3. Pull vacuum to 500 microns, hold for 15 min. 4. Weigh in factory charge per nameplate. 5. Adjust for line set length (typically +0.6 oz per foot over 25ft for R-410A). 6. Verify superheat and subcooling after charge.
commonMistakes: Adding refrigerant without finding leak - customer callback guaranteed
Charging by pressure alone instead of weighing in or using superheat/subcool method
Not pulling vacuum after repair - moisture contamination
Not checking for restrictions (filter drier, TXV) that mimic low charge

diagnosticSteps: Visual inspection of condenser coil - look for matted debris, cottonwood, grass clippings
Check discharge pressure - will be elevated above normal
Check subcooling - may be high (>20°F) due to liquid backing up
Check condenser split: ambient temp vs condensing temp - should be 15-25°F, dirty coil shows >30°F
Check amp draw - will be elevated due to high head pressure
rootCauses: Normal environmental debris (cottonwood, dust, pollen)
Pet hair accumulation
Landscaping too close to unit (needs 24" clearance minimum)
Lack of annual maintenance
entries.repairProcedure: 1. Turn off system. 2. Remove top grille/fan assembly if needed. 3. Spray coil cleaner (Nu-Calgon or equivalent) from inside out. 4. Let soak 5-10 minutes. 5. Rinse with garden hose from inside out - never use pressure washer (bends fins). 6. Straighten any bent fins with fin comb. 7. Verify amp draw and pressures return to normal.

diagnosticSteps: Check filter - hold up to light, if no light passes through it's too dirty
Check static pressure across filter - should be < 0.3" WC for 1" filter
Check temperature split across coil - should be 16-22°F cooling
Low airflow causes: suction pressure drops, superheat increases, coil may frost
entries.repairProcedure: Replace filter. Educate customer on filter change interval (30-90 days depending on type). If coil is frozen, turn system to fan-only for 2-4 hours to defrost before restarting.

diagnosticSteps: Check for 24V across contactor coil - should pull in when thermostat calls
Visual inspect contacts - look for pitting, arcing damage, or welded contacts
With contactor pulled in, check voltage across load-side contacts - should be <1V (near zero)
If >3V across closed contacts, replace contactor (resistance = heat)
Check for chattering - weak coil or low control voltage
Welded contactor: unit won't shut off, runs continuously
rootCauses: Normal wear from electrical arcing (30,000-100,000 cycles lifespan)
Low 24V control voltage causing weak pull-in (chattering)
Insect nests in contactor housing (ants are common)
Pitted contacts from inrush current
entries.repairProcedure: Replace contactor with same coil voltage (24V) and amp rating. Replace both if dual contactor setup. Check control voltage (24V transformer) while replacing. Clean housing of any debris.

symptoms: Unit runs but no temperature change
diagnosticSteps: Check suction line - ice or heavy condensation/frost confirms freezing
Check filter first - dirty filter is #1 cause
Check blower operation - is it running? Correct speed?
Check return air path - all registers open? Ductwork collapsed?
If airflow is good, check refrigerant charge - low charge can cause freeze too
Check TXV operation if equipped - stuck open causes flooding and freeze
Measure suction pressure - should match saturation temp above 32°F
rootCauses: Restricted airflow (dirty filter, closed registers, collapsed duct) - 70% of cases
Low refrigerant charge - 20% of cases
Blower motor failure or wrong speed setting - 5%
TXV stuck open or overfeeding - 5%
Running A/C below 60°F outdoor temp without low-ambient kit
entries.repairProcedure: 1. Turn system to FAN ONLY or OFF to defrost (2-4 hours). 2. Do NOT scrape ice off coil - damages fins. 3. Once defrosted, diagnose root cause. 4. Replace filter if dirty. 5. Check charge and airflow. 6. Restart and monitor for 15 min.
commonMistakes: Trying to run system while coil is frozen - can slug compressor with liquid
Adding refrigerant to a frozen system without defrosting first - readings will be inaccurate
Not finding root cause - coil will freeze again

diagnosticSteps: BEFORE condemning compressor, ALWAYS check: capacitor, contactor, supply voltage, wiring
Check compressor windings with ohmmeter: C-R, C-S, R-S (R+S should equal C-R + C-S within 3%)
Check each winding to ground - any reading less than infinity = grounded compressor
Check amp draw: compare to RLA on nameplate - LRA on startup is normal for 0.5 sec
If drawing LRA continuously = locked rotor (mechanical seizure)
If open winding (infinite ohms between terminals) = open winding failure
Check crankcase heater operation - oil logging can cause liquid slugging on startup
rootCauses: Liquid slugging from flooded starts (no crankcase heater or TXV issue)
Loss of lubrication from refrigerant leak
Electrical failure from voltage issues or short cycling
Contaminated system (moisture, acid, debris from previous burnout)
Age - typical compressor life 12-20 years
entries.repairProcedure: 1. Confirm compressor is truly failed (not cap, contactor, or wiring). 2. If scroll compressor, check for reverse rotation (swapped wires). 3. If replacing: recover refrigerant, install filter drier, triple-evacuate, weigh in charge. 4. If burnout, flush lines with Rx-11 or equivalent. 5. Add burnout drier. 6. Recheck after 48 hours of operation.
commonMistakes: Condemning compressor when capacitor was the actual problem - #1 misdiagnosis in HVAC
Not checking voltage and wiring before condemning
Not flushing system after burnout - contaminates new compressor
Not installing new filter drier with compressor replacement

diagnosticSteps: Check superheat at evaporator outlet - should be 8-12°F for TXV system
Very low superheat (<3°F) = TXV stuck open / overfeeding → flooding coil, risk of slugging compressor
Very high superheat (>20°F) = TXV stuck closed / restricted → starving coil
Check subcooling at condenser - should be 10-15°F with TXV
Check TXV sensing bulb - must be firmly clamped to suction line with good thermal contact
Check bulb insulation - must be insulated from ambient air
Tap TXV body gently with wrench - sometimes frees stuck valve temporarily
rootCauses: Sensing bulb lost charge (capillary tube leak)
Debris/wax plugging valve seat
Moisture freeze-up at valve seat (inadequate vacuum before charge)
Wrong TXV size for tonnage
Sensing bulb improperly mounted or not insulated
entries.repairProcedure: 1. Verify sensing bulb position and insulation first (free fix if that's the issue). 2. If valve is failed: recover charge, braze in new TXV matched to tonnage and refrigerant. 3. Install new filter drier. 4. Evacuate to 500 microns. 5. Weigh in charge. 6. Verify superheat and subcooling after 15 min of operation.

diagnosticSteps: Check for voltage at motor leads - should have line voltage (120V or 240V depending on motor)
PSC motor: check run capacitor first - most common cause of 'dead' motor
ECM/variable speed motor: check for fault codes on module LED
Spin motor shaft by hand - should turn freely. If stiff, bearings failed
Check amp draw - above nameplate FLA = motor overloaded or failing
Check blower wheel for debris, balance, setscrew loose on shaft
rootCauses: Bad run capacitor (PSC motors) - check this FIRST
Worn bearings from age
ECM control module failure (motor itself may be fine)
Overheating from restricted airflow (dirty filter, dirty blower wheel)
Voltage issues
entries.repairProcedure: PSC motor: test and replace capacitor first ($10 fix vs $300 motor). ECM motor: try power cycling module first. If motor truly failed: match HP, RPM, rotation, shaft size, and mounting. Verify correct speed tap for application.

diagnosticSteps: System cools when it should heat (or vice versa) - valve stuck in wrong position
Both suction and discharge lines same temperature = valve body leaking internally
Check 24V solenoid coil - should energize/de-energize on mode change
Check for pilot valve operation - should hear click when solenoid changes state
Measure temp difference across valve - if all 4 ports similar temp = internal leak
Check system pressures - equalized pressures may prevent valve from shifting
rootCauses: Internal bypass from worn valve seat
Solenoid coil burned out
Pilot valve stuck from debris
Insufficient pressure differential to shift valve (low charge)
entries.repairProcedure: 1. Try energizing/de-energizing solenoid manually. 2. If solenoid clicks but valve doesn't shift: check charge level, try tapping valve body. 3. If internal leak: valve must be replaced (brazed into system). 4. Recovery, replace, evacuate, recharge. Very labor-intensive repair.

symptoms: Yellow/flickering burner flame instead of blue
Soot accumulation around burners or vent
Rust or scale flakes on burners
Visible cracks or holes in heat exchanger surface
Furnace short cycling on flame rollout switch
diagnosticSteps: SAFETY FIRST: If CO suspected, evacuate occupants and ventilate before testing
Use combustion analyzer at flue - CO levels above 100 ppm air-free indicate problem
Visual inspection with inspection mirror and borescope/inspection camera through burner opening
Light burners and observe flame pattern - flame should be steady blue cone
Turn on blower (G call only, no W) - watch for flame disturbance, flickering, or roll-out
Pressure test: cap flue and pressurize cold side to 0.5" WC, watch for pressure drop
Smoke test: introduce smoke into return air with blower on, watch for smoke at burners
Check primary heat exchanger tubes (clamshell or tubular) at bends - most common crack location
Check secondary heat exchanger (90%+ furnaces) for corrosion holes - condensate-related
Tape test: place tissue paper at burners during blower operation - movement indicates breach
Document findings with photos - crack confirmation requires furnace shutdown
rootCauses: Thermal stress fatigue from repeated heating/cooling cycles (primary cause - 15-25 year typical life)
Oversized furnace causing short cycling and excessive expansion/contraction
Restricted airflow causing overheating (dirty filter, undersized return)
Condensate corrosion on secondary heat exchanger (high-efficiency units)
Improper venting causing flue gas condensation in primary heat exchanger
Cracked or warped from delayed ignition explosions
Manufacturing defect in early model years (some recalls exist - check serial number)
entries.repairProcedure: Heat exchanger replacement is rarely cost-effective - typically 50-70% of cost of new furnace. RED-TAG the unit and shut off gas immediately if confirmed crack. Document with photos. Options: 1) Replace heat exchanger (if under warranty - some have 20-year or lifetime parts coverage). 2) Replace entire furnace (recommended on units >12 years old). 3) NEVER continue operating a cracked heat exchanger - life safety issue. Install CO detectors on every level if not present.
entries.estimatedTime: 6-10 hours (heat exchanger swap) or 1 day (full furnace replace)
commonMistakes: Using only visual inspection without combustion analyzer - many cracks are not visible
Not red-tagging unit when crack confirmed - liability and safety issue
Confusing rust/scale with actual crack - use camera and pressure test to verify
Telling customer might be cracked without confirmation - causes panic or false alarm
Not checking root cause (oversized unit, restricted airflow) - new HX will fail too
Forgetting to install/verify CO detectors before leaving job

symptoms: Water staining on ceiling below attic unit
System shut off by float switch
AC won't turn on (float switch open)
Algae visible at drain line termination
diagnosticSteps: Check primary drain pan for standing water - confirms drain restriction
Check secondary drain pan (under air handler) for water - means primary failed
Locate float switch - safety switch in primary pan or in drain line tee
Test float switch: lift float manually with system calling for cooling - should kill 24V
Check drain line slope - minimum 1/8 inch per foot, no sags or bellies
Inspect drain line termination outside - look for algae, debris, or insects
Check P-trap - should be properly sized and primed (water-filled)
Verify trap depth - must be deeper than negative pressure of blower (typically 2-3 inch minimum)
Look for missing trap entirely - common DIY mistake causes drainage issues
Check for biological growth (algae/slime) in pan, drain pan tablet residue indicates neglect
Inspect coil drain pan for rust holes or cracks - secondary leak source
rootCauses: Algae and biological slime growth blocking drain (most common - dark, moist environment)
Dust/debris accumulation in drain line over years
Improper drain line slope or sagging PVC
Missing or improperly sized P-trap (cannot drain against blower negative pressure)
Disconnected drain line at fittings (vibration over time)
Frozen drain line in attic during winter (incomplete insulation)
Insects/wasps building nests in drain termination outside
Rusted-through drain pan (older units, especially horizontal coils)
Failed float switch stuck closed (water keeps rising past safety)
entries.repairProcedure: 1. Shut off system at thermostat. 2. Locate cleanout tee in drain line near air handler. 3. Use wet/dry vac on outdoor termination - pull suction for 1-2 minutes to clear blockage. 4. Alternative: blow out with nitrogen at low pressure (5-10 psi MAX - higher pressure damages pan). 5. Flush with 50/50 distilled vinegar/water OR dilute bleach (1:16) - vinegar is safer and recommended. 6. Some pros prefer pan tablets (Pan-Pro or similar) for ongoing prevention. 7. Verify drainage by pouring 1 gallon water into pan. 8. Check P-trap is primed. 9. Test float switch by manually lifting. 10. Inspect drain pan for rust/damage - replace if compromised. 11. Recommend customer pour 1 cup vinegar in drain monthly during cooling season.
commonMistakes: Using high-pressure nitrogen or compressed air - can crack drain pan or blow joints apart
Using straight bleach - corrodes coil and pan over time, damages aluminum
Skipping the P-trap - water won't drain against blower suction
Not flushing the pan itself - just clears line, biological growth returns quickly
Bypassing float switch instead of fixing drainage - guaranteed water damage
Not checking secondary pan / safety pan in attic installations
Forgetting to prime trap after service - trap won't seal against negative pressure

symptoms: Ignitor glows weakly or not at all
diagnosticSteps: Initiate heat call at thermostat and observe ignition sequence
Watch for ignitor glow through inspection port - should glow bright orange/white within 15-45 seconds
If no glow: shut off power, remove ignitor (be GENTLE - very brittle)
Visual inspect for hairline cracks - cracked ignitor will not heat properly
Check resistance with ohmmeter at ignitor terminals (disconnected from board)
Silicon Carbide (SiC) ignitor: 40-90 ohms cold (older style, more fragile, gray color)
Silicon Nitride (SiN) ignitor: 50-400 ohms cold (newer style, more durable, white/cream color)
Open circuit (OL reading) = failed ignitor, replace
Check supply voltage at ignitor wires during call: should be 120V (or 24V on some models)
If voltage is correct but ignitor does not glow = ignitor failed
If no voltage to ignitor: check control board ignitor relay, pressure switch closed, limit switches
rootCauses: Normal end-of-life from thermal cycling (5-7 years SiC, 10+ years SiN typical)
Physical damage from cleaning/handling (oils from skin contact accelerate failure)
Vibration cracks during furnace operation
Voltage spikes from electrical issues
Improper gap or position causing arcing
Contamination from dust/silicone/cleaning chemicals
entries.repairProcedure: 1. Shut off power at disconnect AND gas supply. 2. Remove burner compartment door. 3. Disconnect ignitor wire harness. 4. Remove ignitor mounting screw (usually 1/4 inch hex head). 5. NEVER touch ignitor element with bare fingers - skin oils cause hot spots and premature failure. 6. Install new ignitor - match by part number or universal kit. 7. Ensure proper position (ignitor should be in center of pilot/burner port). 8. Reconnect wiring. 9. Restore gas and power. 10. Initiate heat call and verify ignition sequence. 11. Check flame pattern after ignition. 12. Recommend SiN upgrade if replacing SiC for longer life.
commonMistakes: Touching ignitor element with bare hands - oils cause early failure
Cross-threading the mounting screw - cracks ceramic base
Not checking pressure switch and limit switches first - they prevent ignitor power
Installing wrong ignitor type for furnace model
Bending ignitor leads to fit - causes stress fractures
Not addressing root cause if multiple failures (voltage issues, vibration source)

symptoms: Loud humming or grinding from inducer
Inducer runs but burners don't light
No draft proving / pressure switch never closes
diagnosticSteps: Initiate heat call - inducer should start FIRST (pre-purge cycle, 15-30 seconds)
Listen for inducer motor: if dead silent = no power or failed motor
Check for 120V at inducer motor leads during call
If voltage present but no spin: motor is failed (or seized bearings)
If inducer runs but pressure switch never closes: weak motor, blocked vent, or stuck switch
Check pressure switch hose for water, kinks, or disconnection
Measure pressure switch with manometer at hose port: typical -0.50 to -1.80 inches WC
Below threshold reading = inducer not creating enough draft
Spin motor by hand (power off): should turn smoothly, no grinding
Check motor capacitor if PSC inducer (some models)
Check vent pipe for obstructions: bird nests, ice blockage, condensate
Check secondary heat exchanger drain on 90%+ units - clogged drain backs water into pressure switch hose
rootCauses: Bearing failure from age and continuous cycling (most common - 10-15 year life)
Capacitor failure on PSC inducer motors (test cap first)
Burned windings from voltage issues or restricted vent
Wheel imbalance from corrosion or debris
Cracked motor housing allowing air leak
Failed pressure switch mistaken for inducer failure
Blocked vent pipe causing motor to overwork and overheat
Water in pressure switch hose preventing proper draft sensing
entries.repairProcedure: 1. Shut off power and gas. 2. Disconnect motor wiring (note polarity). 3. Disconnect pressure switch hose from inducer port. 4. Remove inducer assembly mounting screws. 5. Note gasket condition - replace if compromised (combustion gas leak hazard). 6. Install new inducer assembly with new gasket. 7. Reconnect wiring and pressure hose. 8. Restore power and gas. 9. Initiate heat call - verify pressure switch closes and ignition occurs. 10. Verify proper draft with manometer if possible. 11. Check for vent leaks around new gasket.
commonMistakes: Replacing inducer when pressure switch was the failed component
Forgetting to replace gasket - flue gas leak risk
Not checking vent pipe for blockage - new motor will fail too
Not draining secondary heat exchanger trap on 90%+ furnaces - water returns to pressure switch
Wrong rotation direction on universal replacement
Cross-wiring leads on motors with multiple speeds

diagnosticSteps: Visual inspect coil through service port or by pulling cabinet panel
Look for matted dust between fins, often in 1/8 inch thick layer
Check coil entering and leaving sides - dirt usually accumulates on entering air side
Measure static pressure across coil - should be <0.3 inches WC, dirty coil shows >0.5 inches WC
Check temperature split: should be 16-22 degrees F across coil (cooling), low delta-T from poor airflow
Check superheat: low superheat (<5 degrees F) can indicate flooded coil from poor airflow
Check suction pressure: lower than normal due to reduced load on coil
Compare blower amp draw to nameplate FLA - high amps = motor working harder
Inspect for biological growth - black/green discoloration on aluminum fins
Check filter history - dirty coils usually result from poor filter maintenance
rootCauses: Inadequate filter maintenance allowing dust through to coil (primary cause)
Bypass air around filter (poor filter rack seal)
Cheap fiberglass filters with low MERV not capturing fine particles
High pet dander or smoking environment
Construction debris from remodeling project
No filter present (DIY removal)
Biological growth from chronic moisture and lack of UV light
Improper installation allowing return-side dust ingress
entries.repairProcedure: 1. Shut off power and tag out at disconnect. 2. Access coil - remove cabinet panels or A-coil access plate. 3. Protect drain pan and surrounding area with plastic and rags. 4. For light dirt: brush from leaving air side with soft brush, then vacuum. 5. For heavy dirt or biological growth: use coil cleaner. 6. ALKALINE cleaner (Nu-Calgon Evap Pow'r or similar) for general dirt and oils - foaming action lifts dirt. 7. ACID cleaner for severe corrosion staining or mineral deposits - use with EXTREME caution, full PPE. 8. NEVER use acid cleaner on aluminum micro-channel coils - destroys coating. 9. Apply cleaner per directions, allow dwell time (usually 5-10 min). 10. Rinse THOROUGHLY with low-pressure water - chemical residue corrodes coil. 11. Verify drain pan and line clear before restoring power. 12. Recommend UV light installation to prevent biological regrowth.
commonMistakes: Using acid cleaner on aluminum micro-channel coils - permanently damages
Not protecting drain pan/electronics during cleaning - water damage
Skipping rinse step - chemical residue continues corroding coil
Using too much pressure on rinse - bends fins flat
Not addressing filter issue - coil will be dirty again in months
Not testing system after cleaning to verify proper temperature split

symptoms: No gas to burners despite ignition attempt
Furnace locks out after ignition trials
Click from gas valve but no flame
Pilot won't stay lit (older standing pilot units)
diagnosticSteps: SAFETY: Use gas leak detector and soap solution before starting work
Initiate heat call and observe ignition sequence through complete cycle
After inducer purge and ignitor warm-up, check for 24V at gas valve terminals during call
Use voltmeter on MV (main valve) and PV (pilot valve, if applicable) terminals
If no 24V at valve during call: control board, flame sensor, or rollout switch issue
If 24V present at valve but no gas flow: gas valve is failed
Check inlet gas pressure with manometer at inlet tap (typical 7 inches WC for natural, 11 inches WC for LP)
Check outlet/manifold pressure at outlet tap during burn (typical 3.5 inches WC NG, 10 inches WC LP)
Outlet pressure too low or zero with valve energized = failed valve
Outlet pressure unstable/fluctuating = failing pressure regulator section
Test high-fire and low-fire pressures on two-stage valves
Verify wiring at valve - terminals labeled MV, MV/PV, PV, TH, TR (24V common terminology)
rootCauses: Internal solenoid coil failure (no gas flow despite voltage)
Diaphragm failure in regulator section (incorrect outlet pressure)
Foreign material lodged in valve seat (debris from supply line)
Corrosion from moisture infiltration
Lockout from internal safety after multiple failed ignition attempts
Wrong gas type conversion (NG vs LP) without orifice/regulator change
Voltage spike or board failure damaging valve solenoid
Age - 15-20 year typical valve life
entries.repairProcedure: 1. Shut off gas at upstream shutoff and electrical disconnect. 2. Document existing wiring with photo. 3. Disconnect 24V wiring from valve. 4. Disconnect gas piping (use two wrenches to avoid damaging valve - back-up wrench essential). 5. Remove old valve. 6. Apply gas-rated thread sealant (yellow Teflon tape rated for gas, or pipe dope) - never use white Teflon on gas. 7. Install new valve - VERIFY arrow on body shows correct flow direction. 8. Match valve type: single-stage, two-stage, or modulating. 9. Verify it matches gas type (NG or LP). 10. Reconnect wiring per labeled terminals. 11. Pressurize and leak-check ALL fittings with soap solution and electronic detector. 12. Power up and test through complete heat cycle. 13. Verify manifold pressure at outlet tap matches nameplate spec. 14. Final leak check after temperature rise. 15. Verify CO levels with combustion analyzer.
commonMistakes: Replacing valve without checking that voltage is reaching it - wasted part
Using wrong thread sealant on gas connections - leak hazard
Not verifying manifold pressure after install - over/under-firing causes other failures
Wrong valve type for gas (NG/LP) or stage configuration
Not checking inlet pressure first - low supply pressure mimics valve failure
Skipping comprehensive leak check after install - life safety issue
Forgetting to remove plastic shipping plug from inlet/outlet ports
Not verifying CO levels post-repair with combustion analyzer

symptoms: Outdoor coil completely iced over in heating mode
Heat pump stuck in defrost mode (running cooling outdoors)
No defrost cycle initiating during heating
Loud whoosh of reversing valve at random intervals
Heat strips coming on without defrost activation
Reduced heating capacity in cold weather
Excessive ice buildup damaging fan blades
diagnosticSteps: Verify problem is defrost-related: outdoor coil heavily iced in heating mode confirms
Check defrost timer settings on board: typically 30, 60, or 90 minute intervals
Locate defrost board - usually in outdoor unit control box
Initiate forced defrost: short test pins on board (TEST/SPEEDUP pins) per manufacturer
Watch for proper sequence: reversing valve clicks, outdoor fan stops, aux heat energizes
Time normal defrost cycle: 5-10 minutes typical, terminates by temp or 10-min max time
Check defrost thermostat (clamped to liquid line at coil) - opens at 32 degrees F, closes at 80 degrees F
Test defrost thermostat with ohmmeter: should be closed below 32 degrees F, open above 80 degrees F
Verify board outputs: 24V to reversing valve solenoid during defrost call
Check W2/aux heat output during defrost - prevents cold air discharge indoors
Inspect board for burn marks, swollen capacitors, or corrosion
Some boards have LED diagnostics - decode flash patterns per manufacturer
rootCauses: Failed defrost board electronics (relay or processor failure)
Defrost thermostat (sensor) failed - stuck open or closed
Defrost sensor not making good contact with liquid line
Loose or corroded connections at board terminals
Voltage spike damage from lightning or grid issues
Moisture intrusion into outdoor control box
Board age (typically 10-15 year life)
Insect damage to circuit board (ants, spiders nesting)
entries.repairProcedure: Defrost cycle background: heat pump runs in cooling mode briefly to melt ice off outdoor coil, then returns to heating. Cycle initiates when defrost thermostat senses coil is cold AND timer interval has elapsed (demand defrost on newer units uses pressure or temp differential). 1. Shut off power at disconnect. 2. Photograph existing wiring. 3. Note model and revision of board. 4. Replace with EXACT match or universal board with proper jumper settings. 5. Universal boards: configure timer (30/60/90 min), match terminal layout, set heat pump type. 6. Reconnect all wiring per labels. 7. Test defrost via TEST pins - verify proper sequence. 8. Allow normal operation in heating mode and observe a natural defrost cycle.
commonMistakes: Replacing board when defrost sensor was actually failed (much cheaper part)
Wrong jumper settings on universal board - causes too-frequent or no defrosts
Not checking defrost sensor mounting/contact - intermittent issues persist
Mistaking ice from low charge for defrost board issue
Not testing forced defrost cycle after replacement
Not checking outdoor fan motor capacitor - sometimes weak fan causes ice issues
Forgetting to seal control box after service - moisture causes recurring failures

symptoms: Liquid line cold/sweating downstream of drier
Frost forming on liquid line at drier outlet
Unit appears low on charge but is properly charged
Compressor short cycling on low pressure
diagnosticSteps: Connect gauges and verify charge by superheat/subcooling method
Check superheat: high superheat (>20 degrees F TXV system) suggests starved evaporator
Check subcooling: high subcooling (>15 degrees F) suggests liquid restriction backing up
Measure temperature at drier inlet AND outlet using clamp-on thermometer or IR gun
Normal: <2 degrees F temperature drop across drier
5-10 degree F drop = restriction beginning to develop
>10 degree F drop = significant restriction confirmed
Look/feel for frost or sweating at drier outlet - cold spot indicates pressure drop
Compare to previous service records - new restriction or progressive issue
Listen for unusual flow sound (hissing) at drier indicating high pressure drop
rootCauses: Moisture saturation - desiccant beads expand and crumble (most common after extended operation with leak)
Burnout debris from compressor failure passing through system
Brazing scale and copper oxide from improper installation (no nitrogen purge)
System contamination from improper charging procedures
Drier age - desiccant capacity exhausted (typically install new with any major service)
Wrong drier size for system tonnage
Bi-flow drier installed backward in heat pump system
Acid contamination from previous compressor failure
entries.repairProcedure: 1. Recover all refrigerant per EPA standards. 2. Cut out failed drier (do NOT unsweat with torch - may release acid/contamination). 3. Install new drier - match BTU rating (e.g., 084S = 4-ton). 4. CRITICAL: install with arrow pointing toward TXV/metering device (flow direction). 5. For heat pumps: install BI-FLOW drier (no flow direction) or two parallel driers with check valves. 6. Braze with nitrogen purge at 2-5 SCFH to prevent oxide formation inside tubing. 7. Pull deep vacuum to 500 microns minimum. 8. Triple-evacuate if moisture suspected. 9. Weigh in factory charge per nameplate. 10. Verify proper superheat and subcooling. 11. Re-check temperature drop across new drier - should be <2 degrees F.
commonMistakes: Installing drier backward (arrow direction wrong) - immediately restricts flow
Using one-way drier in heat pump - blocks reverse flow
Not purging with nitrogen during brazing - creates new oxide contamination
Inadequate vacuum after install - moisture immediately saturates new drier
Wrong drier size for system tonnage - too small saturates quickly
Not addressing root cause (leak, burnout, contamination) - new drier fails fast
Not weighing in charge - leaving system over or undercharged

symptoms: Motor module LED showing fault code
Fan on continuous low speed in cooling mode
No airflow despite contactor pulled in
diagnosticSteps: Identify motor type: ECM (Electronically Commutated) vs PSC (Permanent Split Capacitor)
ECM identifiers: 16-pin connector to control module, no run capacitor, multiple speed taps via communication
ECM types: GE/Genteq ECM 2.3, ECM 3.0, X13 (constant torque), and variable-speed (full ECM)
X13 motor: simpler, accepts 24V signal on speed taps - easier to troubleshoot
Full ECM (variable speed): receives complex PWM signals from furnace board
Locate motor module - separate housing bolted to motor end (can be replaced separately on most ECMs)
Check for module LED status: typically flashes diagnostic codes
Common LED codes: solid = OK, slow flash = no demand, rapid flash = fault
Verify 24V signals at motor harness during call - check pins per wiring diagram
Power-cycle the system at disconnect - sometimes resets a hung module
Test motor windings independently: separate motor from module, check 3-phase windings (~1-3 ohm balanced)
If windings good but module faulted: replace module only ($150-300 vs $600+ for full motor)
rootCauses: Module electronics failure from age or voltage spike (most common)
Moisture intrusion into module housing - water/condensate damage
Power surge or lightning damage to electronics
Communication wire damage (mice chewing, vibration breaking solder joints)
Wrong replacement module for motor model
Heat damage from restricted airflow or blocked drain
Voltage issues - ECMs sensitive to voltage outside 187-253V range
entries.repairProcedure: ECM vs PSC overview: PSC motors are simpler, capacitor-driven, fixed RPM per tap selection - replace as a unit. ECM motors have a separate module (control board) bolted to the motor body that can often be replaced independently. 1. Identify motor model (sticker on motor body - GE/Genteq/Regal Beloit) and HP rating. 2. Determine if module-only replacement is possible (true on most GE/Genteq ECMs). 3. Shut off power at disconnect. 4. Disconnect motor from electrical and control wiring (photograph orientation first). 5. Remove module retaining bolts (typically 3 hex screws). 6. Slide module off motor end. 7. Install new module - it MUST match motor model number (programmed to specific motor). 8. Reconnect harness - communications and high voltage. 9. Restore power and run through cooling and heating modes. 10. Verify CFM by measuring static pressure or using flow hood.
commonMistakes: Assuming motor failure when only the module is bad - wasting customer's money on full motor
Installing wrong module - they're motor-specific, not universal
Not checking for moisture damage source - new module fails too
Confusing ECM with PSC and trying to test with capacitor
Not verifying CFM after replacement - wrong programming = wrong airflow
Not addressing voltage issues - new module dies the same way

symptoms: Higher than normal subcooling (>15 degrees F)
Compressor short cycling on high pressure
Liquid slugging sounds at compressor startup
Warm air from registers despite running
diagnosticSteps: Connect manifold gauges and record suction and discharge pressures
Calculate subcooling: condensing saturation temp minus liquid line temp
High subcooling (>15 degrees F on TXV system, >12 degrees F on piston) indicates overcharge
Calculate superheat: low superheat (<5 degrees F) on overcharged systems
Compare discharge pressure to ambient: should be ambient + 30-50 degrees F as condensing temp
Discharge pressure 50+ PSIG above expected = overcharge or restriction
Check ambient conditions: high ambient also raises pressures (rule out)
Check airflow across condenser coil - dirty coil mimics overcharge
Check amp draw at compressor - elevated above RLA from high head pressure
Listen at compressor for slugging sounds (knocking, liquid hammer)
Review service history - was charge weighed in or topped off?
rootCauses: Tech topping off charge by pressure rather than weighing in (most common)
Adding refrigerant on cool day then heat returns and pressures spike
Wrong charge calculation (line set length not accounted for)
Charging a flooded system - liquid going into low side increased mass
Multiple service calls each adding a little more
Wrong refrigerant scale calibration during charge weigh-in
entries.repairProcedure: Overcharge consequences: liquid refrigerant can return to compressor (flooding/slugging), washing oil from bearings → premature compressor failure. 1. Connect recovery machine and recovery cylinder. 2. Recover small amounts incrementally - 4-8 oz at a time. 3. Allow system to stabilize 5-10 minutes between recovery. 4. Recheck superheat and subcooling. 5. Target factory subcooling per nameplate (typically 8-12 degrees F for TXV). 6. Consider full recovery and weigh-in if overcharge is significant. 7. If full recovery: pull vacuum to 500 microns. 8. Weigh in factory charge plus line set adjustment. 9. Run system 15+ minutes at design conditions before final readings. 10. Document final superheat, subcooling, and pressures on service ticket.
commonMistakes: Releasing refrigerant to atmosphere instead of proper recovery (EPA violation, $44,539 fine per violation)
Removing too much at once - now system is undercharged
Not recording amount removed for service records
Adding refrigerant to overcharged system thinking it was low
Not weighing for verification - estimating by gauge
Failing to address why system was overcharged (training issue, gauge error)

symptoms: Furnace fires briefly then shuts down
Burners light, run a few minutes, then shut off
Blower runs continuously after burners shut off
Cycling on limit (short cycling on heat)
Furnace lockout after multiple limit trips
diagnosticSteps: Identify limit switch type: auto-reset bimetal disc or manual-reset (rollout switches typically manual)
Locate primary high-limit (mounted on heat exchanger or supply plenum)
Note temperature rating - typically 160-200 degrees F for primary limit
Initiate heat call and monitor: how long do burners run before limit trips?
Measure temperature rise: supply temp minus return temp
Should match nameplate temperature rise spec (typically 35-65 degrees F range)
Excessive temp rise (>spec) = airflow problem or overfired furnace
Check filter - dirty filter is most common limit trip cause
Check evaporator coil for restriction or icing
Check ductwork: closed dampers, registers blocked, kinked flex duct
Verify blower speed tap is correct for cooling and heating modes
Test limit switch with ohmmeter cold: should be closed (continuity)
Check secondary/rollout limits in burner area - flame rollout indicates blocked flue or HX issue
Verify gas pressure/manifold pressure - over-firing causes overheating
rootCauses: Restricted airflow - dirty filter (#1 cause - 60% of cases)
Dirty blower wheel reducing CFM
Closed/blocked supply registers or return grilles
Failed/slow blower motor or wrong speed tap
Collapsed flexible duct in attic
Oversized furnace creating excess heat for ductwork
Overfired due to wrong gas pressure or wrong gas type
Failed limit switch (intermittent or weak bimetal)
Heat exchanger crack causing localized hot spots
entries.repairProcedure: Auto-reset vs manual-reset: Auto-reset (bimetal disc) self-restores when temp drops - keeps tripping if root cause not fixed. Manual-reset (button on top) requires physical reset - typically rollout safeties. Manual-reset trip means SERIOUS issue (HX crack, blocked flue) - investigate thoroughly. 1. NEVER bypass a manual-reset limit. 2. First check filter and replace if dirty. 3. Check blower wheel - clean if dirty. 4. Verify blower speed tap matches install requirements. 5. Measure CFM via static pressure if possible (target 400 CFM/ton heating). 6. Check temperature rise across furnace - must be within nameplate range. 7. If temperature rise high: increase blower speed, clean coil, check ductwork. 8. Replace limit switch only after ruling out airflow issues.
commonMistakes: Replacing limit switch without addressing airflow - same problem returns
Bypassing manual-reset limit - bypasses safety, fire/CO risk
Wrong limit temperature rating - nuisance trips or no protection
Not measuring temperature rise to confirm root cause
Forgetting to check heat exchanger for cracks - especially if rollout tripped
Setting blower speed too high - causes cold drafts

symptoms: One zone too hot or too cold
Zone calling but no airflow to that area
All zones receiving air despite single zone call
System short cycling from high static pressure
Damper motor humming but not moving
diagnosticSteps: Identify zone system type: 24V dampers, 3-wire dampers, or pneumatic (commercial)
Common manufacturers: Honeywell TrueZone, Zonex GenX, EWC Ultra-Zone, Aprilaire
Locate zone board - usually in basement/utility room near air handler
Check zone board status LEDs - power, call indicators, fault
Initiate single-zone call from one thermostat
Verify zone board energizes corresponding damper motor
Check 24V at damper motor terminals during call
Observe damper movement - listen for actuator motor running, watch blade rotate
Test damper actuator manually - should move freely when motor coupling disconnected
Check for stuck blade due to corrosion, debris, or warped sheet metal
Check static pressure with all zones closed except smallest - should not exceed 0.7 inches WC
Verify bypass damper opens during high static conditions
Test zone board outputs for equipment (Y, W, G, R, C terminals to air handler/condenser)
rootCauses: Damper motor (actuator) burned out from continuous operation
Mechanical binding from corrosion or debris in damper blade
Broken damper coupling between motor and shaft
Failed zone control board (check fuses on board first)
Stuck bypass damper not relieving pressure (high static damages equipment)
Wiring damage (mice, vibration, age) between board and dampers
Improperly sized system for zoning (small zone causes excessive bypass)
Zone board firmware corruption or memory failure
entries.repairProcedure: Zoning fundamentals: Modern zoning uses motorized dampers in supply duct branches, controlled by a central zone board that responds to multiple thermostats. A bypass damper is critical - when too few zones are open, the bypass relieves excess static pressure into the return to protect equipment. 1. Identify failure mode (board, damper, wiring, bypass). 2. For damper actuator: shut off zone power, disconnect linkage, replace motor (typically $80-200 each). 3. For board failure: photograph wiring, replace with same model, transfer wires per labels. 4. For stuck damper blade: open access panel in duct, free the binding, lubricate pivot points. 5. Verify static pressure with various zone combinations - should never exceed 0.8 inches WC. 6. Test all zones individually after repair.
entries.estimatedTime: 1-3 hours (single component) to 4-8 hours (full board replacement)
commonMistakes: Not checking bypass damper operation - high static pressure damages compressor and blower
Replacing zone board without checking if simple fuse blew on board
Wrong damper actuator type (spring-return vs power-open) - will not function correctly
Bypassing failed dampers by leaving them open - eliminates zoning benefit
Not addressing oversized equipment with small zones - bypass pressure issues persist
Forgetting to check static pressure under various zone scenarios after repair
